title: India's Space Startups Go Global as Defence Demand Surges Past ISRO's Shadow
excerpt: From a single company in 2014 to 440 startups today, India's private space sector is chasing defence contracts and lunar technology — with China firmly in its sights.
body:
• India's private space sector has grown from a single company in 2014 to roughly 440 startups today, with private investment reaching $618.5 million by March 2026 — and founders are now pitching defence, surveillance and lunar capabilities to global clients.
  • At the India Today Conclave Mumbai 2026, space startups showcased surveillance and lunar technology as the next frontier, with companies like Digantara winning government contracts in Singapore and Thailand for space-based surveillance.
  • Prime Minister Narendra Modi met the founders of 20 space-tech startups on National Space Day, urging them to capture a larger share of the $600 billion global space economy and apply space technology to agriculture, climate and disaster management.
  • The ambition is explicit: move from building missions to building enduring companies — and position India as the country the world looks to whenever space is discussed, in direct competition with China.

India's space startups used the India Today Conclave Mumbai 2026 stage this week to make their case as the country's answer to China in orbit — a private sector that has grown from a single company in 2014 to roughly 440 startups today, now chasing global defence and surveillance contracts once reserved for state agencies.

The message from founders at the conclave, held October 9–10 at the Four Seasons Hotel under the theme “Gateway to Growth,” was that India has moved past proving it can reach space cheaply. The harder test now is building companies that can turn that capability into enduring, export-scale businesses — and take on China in the markets that matter.

From launches to surveillance and lunar tech

The startups on show span the full stack. Digantara, the Bengaluru company that raised a $50 million Series B and launched its SCOT surveillance satellite in January, unveiled MOSAIC — an AI-powered optical sensor network designed to autonomously track satellites and space debris in low-Earth orbit — and has inked deals with the governments of Singapore and Thailand. GalaxEye launched its Mission Drishti spacecraft aboard a SpaceX Falcon 9, synchronising optical and synthetic aperture radar sensors to deliver high-resolution, all-weather Earth observation data.

https://youtube.com/watch?v=d6H4rLXuj6g

Agnikul Cosmos has opened testing and inspection facilities in Chennai to validate reusable rocket stages, following the May flight of Agnibaan SorTeD powered by the world's first single-piece 3D-printed engine. Skyroot Aerospace, Pixxel, Dhruva Space and Bellatrix Aerospace round out a cohort that is winning attention for lunar technology and defence-grade surveillance — precisely the capabilities where China has long dominated the Asian market.

Government tailwinds

The sector's momentum has explicit political backing. On National Space Day, Prime Minister Narendra Modi held a high-level interaction in New Delhi with the founders and chief executives of 20 pioneering space-tech startups, pressing them to make India the country the world looks to whenever space is discussed.

“India has shown that it can build sophisticated space capabilities. The next test is building companies that can turn those capabilities into enduring businesses.”

— Industry assessment, via Mint/LinkedIn

Modi urged companies to look beyond conventional applications — space-debris firms working with environmental organisations, space-based agricultural technology with agricultural universities — and set the Bharatiya Antariksha Station, India's planned space station, as a 2035 milestone. India's space agreements with the US, Australia, Japan and the European Union are opening doors to global clients, and strong demand for defence and surveillance satellites is pulling startups toward the military market.

Diaspora angle

For the diaspora's engineers and investors, the numbers tell the story: $618.5 million in private investment by March 2026 and a pipeline of startups selling to foreign governments. The sector is one of the clearest on-ramps for NRI capital and talent into India's deep-tech economy — and for students, a signal that space careers no longer run only through ISRO.

What's next

The gap the startups must still close is the one between working technology and flight heritage — testing, qualification, customers and repeat orders at scale. The less visible parts of the ecosystem, from components and sensors to specialised manufacturing, will decide whether the boom becomes an industry. But with defence demand surging and government contracts flowing, the startups' pitch is no longer “we can do it cheaper” — it's “we can do what China does.”
